CHIEF COMPLAINT
Evaluation of kidney stones.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a previously healthy individual who presented one week ago with sudden onset right-sided back pain while working in the barn moving hay. He initially thought the pain was from the physical activity, but it was accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea, prompting him to seek medical evaluation. His PCP ordered a CT scan which revealed a kidney stone. The pain radiated almost to the groin but not the entire way down. Since the initial presentation, pain has occurred intermittently and is not as prolonged as the initial episode. Patient denies hematuria and reports urine color has not been darker than usual. He has been straining his urine as instructed and has not visualized any stone fragments to date. Denies any prior history of kidney stones.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Patient reports initial episode of diaphoresis and nausea associated with pain. Denies current fever, dysuria, or hematuria.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
No significant past medical history reported.

MEDICATIONS
None reported.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Father had multiple kidney stones.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Works with horses and performs physical labor including hay moving.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital signs: Stable, no fever. Blood pressure and heart rate normal. Abdomen: Soft, no tenderness to palpation, no rebound or guarding. CVA tenderness noted on the right side consistent with kidney inflammation from stone.

RESULTS
CT scan shows a stone measuring 0.5 cm located in the proximal right ureter. No evidence of hydronephrosis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Right ureteral kidney stone, 0.5 cm, proximal right ureter, without obstruction or hydronephrosis. Plan: Increase fluid intake to facilitate spontaneous passage of stone. Start oxycodone 5 mg every 6-8 hours for pain management; may use acetaminophen between doses for breakthrough pain. Continue urine straining until stone passes. Order BMP, urinalysis, and urine culture to assess for infection and renal function. If urinalysis indicates infection, antibiotics will be prescribed. Follow-up appointment in 1-2 weeks. If stone has not passed by that time, discuss further interventions including lithotripsy.
